summary: Summary report of a one-day Chatham-House-rule S3C2 summit (15 Sept 2025) with 10 practitioners from 8 unnamed companies on vulnerable dependencies, component/container choice, malicious commits, build infrastructure, culture, and LLMs in the supply chain. It lists continued themes and new ideas per topic; new LLM-related ideas include tiered agent permissions by developer seniority, agents as first-class identities, and MCP connectors as hidden supply-chain surfaces.

claims.claim: Some organizations block or tightly limit MCP connectors by default because they quietly expand the supply chain into internal repos/documents.
claims.evidence: §7.2 'MCP-driven expansion of hidden supply-chain surfaces'; unattributed, 'some organizations', no count.

claims.claim: Practitioners propose tiered agent access: high-impact agent actions (code changes, workflow coordination) restricted to experienced developers; juniors read-only; agents given explicit identities.
claims.evidence: §7.2 'Identity-aware agentic workflows with tiered access'; proposal from panelists, not an observed practice with outcomes.

claims.claim: Network-isolated CI builds (no egress after dependency fetch) are seen as a more reliable safeguard than reputation scores.
Heavy AI-assisted coding by juniors is widening skill gaps and weakening review culture.

patterns.note: Tiered, identity-aware agent permissions (read-only for juniors) proposed by practitioners (§7.2).
MCP connectors flagged as a supply-chain/data-exfiltration surface; some orgs default-deny (§7.2).
Network-isolated builds and isolated environments for LLM use mentioned (§3.2, §7.1).
Provenance/attestation for agent actions and inference-time provenance (SLSA/GUAC extension) proposed (§5.2, §7.2).
Concern that reliance on model output weakens human review (§6.2, §7.1).

methodology.sample: 10 practitioners from 8 companies, one day; identities withheld.
methodology.baselines: n/a (qualitative); narrative comparison to prior S3C2 summits.

standards.peer_review: None indicated; report reviewed by participants and S3C2 researchers (§1).

biases.detail: Invited companies 'actively engaged in software security'; topics voted by participants.
Researcher notes drafted into themes by a PhD student; no coding protocol, agreement measure, or counts.

coi.affiliations: NC State, Paderborn/George Washington, U. Maryland, CMU (S3C2).

verdict_reason: Practitioner-opinion summary with no systematic method; useful as an idea list (MCP default-deny, agent identities, tiered agent permissions) but provides no evidence that any of these controls work. Fails the rigor floor for a knowledge base meant to weight evidence.
applicability: Idea-level only. For the Java team: treat MCP connectors that can read the ≥4 ingestion repos or internal docs as supply-chain surfaces (default-deny, explicit allow-list per repo), give agent runs distinct identities in CI so provenance of agent-authored commits is auditable across hosts (Cursor/Claude Code/Codex/Hermes), and consider read-only agent modes for less experienced contributors. Healthcare-adjacent data argues for zero-retention provider settings (§7.1). None of this is tested here; nothing on spec-driven development.
